prompt: What does a relationship in the data model do that an `XLOOKUP` column in `Sales` does not?
hint: One of them copies a value; the other says where the value is.

choices.text: It fetches the origin faster, because the model is compiled before a pivot table asks
choices.why: Speed is not the difference the lesson draws. A lookup copies the fact into 108 rows; a relationship copies nothing.

choices.text: It says once which column points at which, and copies nothing into Sales
choices.why: Right. The model follows the pointer each time it adds up a cell, so Sales keeps only the facts about a sale.

choices.text: It replaces the codes in Sales with the names from Products
choices.why: The codes stay exactly as they are. They are what the relationship follows.

choices.text: It works on a Mac as well as on Windows
choices.why: The opposite: Power Pivot, and so the model, exists only in Excel for Windows.

prompt: A colleague answers three new questions by adding an `XLOOKUP` column each to `Sales`: origin, customer type and quarter. What does that cost, in the lesson's terms?
hint: Count the formulas, and ask what kind of column each one is.

choices.text: Nothing: lookup columns are the way the model works inside
choices.why: The model keeps tables apart and copies nothing; lookup columns are what it replaces.

choices.text: 324 formulas, each a copy of a value held elsewhere
choices.why: Right: 108 per column, each one a copy, and Sales now mixes recorded columns with fetched ones nobody can tell apart.

choices.text: The pivot table can no longer group by the three new columns
choices.why: It can. The objection is the copies and the widening, not that the pivot table fails.

choices.text: Excel limits a table to seven columns, and Sales would pass it
choices.why: There is no such limit; a table can have thousands of columns.

prompt: How were the pivot-table results quoted in this lesson produced?
hint: The lesson says it in its second section.

choices.text: By Power Pivot, on Excel for Windows
choices.why: The course was written on a computer with no Excel, and Power Pivot has no engine outside it.

choices.text: By LibreOffice Calc, which reads data models
choices.why: Calc has no data model. It checked the numbers a spreadsheet can check, such as the grand total.

choices.text: They were estimated from the totals of lesson 1
choices.why: Nothing in the course is estimated; every number was computed.

choices.text: By applying the same relationships to the same rows, outside Excel
choices.why: Right, and where a spreadsheet could check a number, such as the grand total, a spreadsheet did.

prompt: Match each table of the model to what it is.
hint: Ask of each: did its row happen, or does it exist?

pairs.right: Fact table, one row per sale

right_distractors: Fact table, one row per product

prompt: Why does `Channel` stay a column of `Sales` rather than get a table of its own?
hint: What does a dimension carry that makes it worth a table?

choices.text: A dimension must have at least ten rows, and Channel has only three values
choices.why: Products has six rows and is a dimension. The size is not the test.

choices.text: A pivot table cannot group rows by a column of the fact table itself
choices.why: It can: Sales[Channel] goes straight into Rows.

choices.text: A Channels table would hold the word and nothing else about it
choices.why: Right. A dimension earns its place by carrying attributes; the day there is a fee per channel to record, it is worth making.

choices.text: Text columns are not allowed in a dimension
choices.why: Dimensions are mostly text: Origin, Roast, Type, City.

prompt: Café Serra starts recording every delivery: the sale it belongs to, the day it left and the driver. Where does that go in the model?
hint: Use the lesson's test: did each row happen, or does it exist?

choices.text: A new column in Products, since deliveries are about products
choices.why: A product exists once; deliveries happen many times. Putting them in Products would break its grain of one row per product.

choices.text: A second fact table, one row per delivery, with keys to Sales or to the dimensions
choices.why: Right. Each row happened, on a date, and there will be many: that is a fact table, and the driver may well become a dimension.

choices.text: Nowhere: a model holds only one fact table
choices.why: A model can hold several fact tables sharing dimensions; the calendar would serve both.

choices.text: A dimension, because drivers are people and people are always dimensions in a model
choices.why: The driver may be a dimension. The delivery is an event with a date, which is what makes it a fact.

prompt: A model where a dimension points at another dimension, such as `Products` at an `Origins` table, is called a ___ rather than a star.
hint: Something that falls in winter, with more branches than a star has points.

prompt: Why does the lesson ask you to check each table's name before adding it to the data model?
hint: The model's table takes a name from somewhere.

choices.text: The model refuses any table whose name begins with a capital letter
choices.why: Sales, Products and Customers all start with a capital and load fine.

choices.text: The model keeps the name, so Table1 would be in every DAX formula
choices.why: Right. Lesson 16's measures would read Table1[Revenue]; a name fixed before loading is one less thing to break.

choices.text: Renaming is impossible once a table has been loaded into the model
choices.why: It is possible later. The lesson's point is that it is cheaper first.

choices.text: The name decides which of the three doors into the model the table uses
choices.why: The door is chosen by you: Add to Data Model, a pivot table, or Power Query.

prompt: After loading the three tables, how many records should the `Customers` tab of the Power Pivot window show?
hint: One row per customer, from `C00` up; the header is not a record.

prompt: You add a sale to the `Sales` table on the sheet. How does it reach the model and the pivot tables built on it?
hint: Think about which side is entered and which side is read.

choices.text: Type it again in the Power Pivot window, on the Sales tab
choices.why: Power Pivot's window does not let you edit a value at all. Records are entered on the sheet.

choices.text: Data › Refresh All, because Sales is a linked table
choices.why: Right. A linked table follows the table on the sheet, and the refresh carries the change to every pivot table too.

choices.text: Delete Sales from the model and load it again from the sheet
choices.why: That works and throws away its relationships with it. A refresh is all it needs.

choices.text: It never does: a model is a snapshot taken when loaded
choices.why: A linked table stays connected to its source; that is the point of loading rather than copying.

prompt: Somebody pasted the `CER1K` row of `Products` twice. When you drag `Sales[Product]` onto `Products[Code]`, Excel will not create the relationship. Why?
hint: Which side of a relationship has a rule about duplicates?

choices.text: Codes with digits in them cannot be keys
choices.why: S1001, C03 and CER1K are all keys with digits. The trouble is the repetition.

choices.text: Sales has many rows for CER1K, and the many side must be unique
choices.why: The many side is allowed repeats; that is why it is called the many side.

choices.text: Products has more columns than Sales, so the direction is wrong
choices.why: Column counts have nothing to do with it. Uniqueness of the key does.

choices.text: A CER1K sale would not know which of two products it meant
choices.why: Right. The one side has to be unique, and both columns now repeat CER1K, so Excel refuses rather than guess.

prompt: With all three relationships in place, a pivot table has `Sales[Channel]` in Rows and Count of Code, from `Products[Code]`, in Values. Every row says 6. Why?
hint: Which way does a filter travel along a relationship?

choices.text: The relationship between Sales and Products is missing
choices.why: Without it you would also see 6, but the lesson's case has it in place. The cause here is direction.

choices.text: Each channel happens to have sold every one of the six products in the catalogue
choices.why: Shop sold fewer than six products; the 6 does not depend on what was sold at all.

choices.text: The channel filter sits on the many side and never climbs back up to Products
choices.why: Right. A filter flows from the one side to the many side. To count per channel, count in Sales, where the channel is.

choices.text: Count only works on numbers, so it counts the header instead
choices.why: Count counts text values; Code has six of them, which is the 6.

prompt: A pivot table on the model has `Products[Origin]` in Rows and Sum of Revenue in Values, and each of the three rows shows R$ 51,494. What is wrong?
hint: 51,494 is a number you have met before.

choices.text: Revenue is formatted as currency, which hides the decimals
choices.why: A format changes how a number looks, not which rows are added.

choices.text: Origin is text, and a pivot table needs a number in Rows
choices.why: Rows are almost always text. Origin is exactly the kind of field that belongs there.

choices.text: There is no relationship between Sales and Products
choices.why: Right. 51,494 is all the revenue there is; with no line between the tables, the Origin filter reaches nothing and each row adds up all of Sales.

choices.text: The calendar has not been marked as the date table
choices.why: That matters for lesson 16's period functions. This pivot table has no date in it at all.

prompt: Which of these are true of the relationship from `Sales[Product]` to `Products[Code]`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Uniqueness, type and direction.

choices.text: Every value of Products[Code] must be unique
choices.why: The one side identifies one row per key, or a sale would not know which product it meant.

choices.text: The two columns must hold the same type of value
choices.why: Text joins text. A code that is text on one side and a number on the other matches nothing.

choices.text: A filter on Products[Origin] reaches the rows of Sales
choices.why: That is the direction a filter flows: from the one side to the many side.

choices.text: A filter on Sales[Channel] reaches the rows of Products
choices.why: It does not climb back to the one side, which is why Count of Code says 6 on every channel row.

prompt: In the pivot table with `Sales[Channel]` in Rows and Count of Code from `Products[Code]` in Values, what does the `Shop` row show?
hint: It does not depend on what the shop sold.

prompt: How many rows does the `Calendar` table have, from 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2026?
The last sale is on 23 June 2026. Why does the calendar still run to 31 December 2026?
hint: What do lesson 16's period functions expect a year to be?

choices.text: Because Excel tables need an even number of rows
choices.why: No such rule exists. The length comes from whole years.

choices.text: So the model has room for sales that have not been typed yet
choices.why: It does give that room, but the lesson's reason is that a year of 2026 must be the same kind of thing as a year of 2025.

choices.text: Period functions expect whole years
choices.why: Right. The price is six months of 2026 with no sales, and lesson 16 section 05 shows what that does to a comparison.

choices.text: Because SEQUENCE always produces whole years
choices.why: SEQUENCE produces as many rows as you ask for; 730 was chosen.

prompt: After `=SEQUENCE(730,1,DATE(2025,1,1),1)` has spilled down column A, why does the lesson paste the days back as values?
hint: What is the next step, and what can it not hold?

choices.text: Because an Excel table cannot hold a formula that spills
choices.why: Right. The days become plain values, and then Insert › Table can turn the block into the Calendar table.

choices.text: Because a spilled formula recalculates to a different date every day
choices.why: SEQUENCE with fixed arguments always gives the same days. The reason is the table.

choices.text: Because the data model cannot read dates, only numbers
choices.why: The model reads dates; Calendar[Date] has to be a Date column.

choices.text: So that the dates show as numbers such as 45658
choices.why: That is a side effect to fix with a date format, not the reason.

prompt: Put the making of the calendar in order, from an empty sheet to a table the model trusts.
hint: The days first, then the table, then the model.
items: Type the SEQUENCE formula in A2 under the header Date
Paste the 730 days back over themselves as values
Insert a table and name it Calendar
Add the Year, Month, Month name and Quarter columns
Load Calendar into the data model
Mark Calendar as the date table
trap: Inserting the table before pasting values fails, because a table cannot hold a formula that spills.

prompt: A till exports sales with the time of day, such as `2025-08-15 14:30`. Loaded into the model and related to `Calendar[Date]`, all its revenue lands on a `(blank)` row. Why?
hint: A date is a count of days. What is a time?

choices.text: The calendar is not marked as the date table
choices.why: Marking checks the calendar's own column. It does not make 14:30 match a whole day.

choices.text: The model cannot hold times of day, so it deletes those values on loading
choices.why: The rows arrive and are counted; that is why the revenue appears on a blank row rather than vanishing.

choices.text: Each value is a day plus a fraction, and no calendar row holds that number
choices.why: Right. The calendar's rows are whole days, so nothing matches; keep only the date, with INT on a sheet or a Date type in Power Query.

choices.text: A till's export always stores its dates as text, whatever the screen shows
choices.why: They may or may not be text. Even as real dates and times, they would not match whole days.

prompt: `Calendar[Month name]` in a pivot table's rows shows `Apr`, `Aug`, `Dec`, `Feb`… How do you get the months in calendar order in every report?
hint: The model can be told that one column sorts by another.

choices.text: Sort the pivot table's rows by hand, from A to Z, in every report
choices.why: A to Z is the alphabetical order you already have; Z to A is no better.

choices.text: Rename the months 01 Jan, 02 Feb and so on
choices.why: It works and puts numbers in every label; the model has a tool made for it.

choices.text: In Power Pivot, sort Month name by the Month column
choices.why: Right: Home › Sort by Column. Every pivot table built on the model then puts Jan first.

choices.text: Mark Calendar as the date table again
choices.why: Marking tells the period functions which column to use. It does not sort text.

prompt: In the pivot table with `Products[Origin]` in Rows, `Calendar[Year]` in Columns and Sum of Revenue in Values, what is the cell for `Cerrado` in 2025, in reais?
hint: Two products, one year.

prompt: With `Customers[State]` in Rows, one row is labelled `(blank)`, with R$ 12,763. What is it?
hint: Look at the first row of Customers.

choices.text: Sales whose customer code is missing from Customers
choices.why: That would also land on a blank row, but every sale's customer exists. Here the state is the empty thing.

choices.text: C00's 70 sales, because the walk-in customer's State is empty
choices.why: Right. The walk-in and web customer has no state, so its revenue is counted under a label that says unknown.

choices.text: Sales from outside Brazil
choices.why: There are none; every customer with a state is in MG, SP, RJ or PR.

choices.text: An error in the relationship that should be deleted
choices.why: Nothing is broken, and deleting the row would lose R$ 12,763 of real revenue.

prompt: Match each thing a model pivot table shows to its most likely cause.
hint: Every one of these was met in the lesson.

pairs.left: The same total on every row
pairs.right: No relationship between the two tables
A value from a dimension, with rows from the facts
A key or an attribute with nothing on the other side
Month name not sorted by Month

prompt: In a pivot table on the model, rows and columns come from dimensions, and values come from the ___ table.
hint: The table whose rows happened.
